courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Why radiance fields needed a rasterizer instead of ray marching
question: A colleague says 3DGS is fast because it uses a smaller neural network than NeRF. What is the more accurate explanation?
options: It uses a hash grid to make the MLP queries cheaper, like InstantNGP
It renders at lower resolution and upsamples the result
It has no network at render time: explicit Gaussians are projected and alpha blended by a sorting rasterizer
It skips the transmittance term, so each sample is independent
explain: 3DGS has no neural network at all. The scene is a list of Gaussians with stored parameters, and rendering is projection plus sorted alpha blending. The blending formula still includes transmittance; it is the same image formation model as NeRF.

courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
question: Compared with Mip-NeRF360, which statement about 3DGS (30K iterations) on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset matches the paper?
options: Higher PSNR, faster training, and a smaller model
Slightly lower PSNR, much faster training and rendering, and a much larger model
Same PSNR and same model size, but faster rendering
Lower quality on every metric, but real-time rendering
explain: Table 1: PSNR 27.21 vs 27.69 dB (slightly lower), but SSIM and LPIPS slightly better, training about 42 minutes vs 48 hours, 134 vs 0.06 FPS, and 734 MB vs 8.6 MB.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
question: In the hazard pointer pop, a developer removes the line that re-checks top.load() != t after announcing t. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the announcement alone protects t
The CAS will always fail
Between reading t and announcing it, t may have been popped, retired and freed by a scan that did not see the announcement, so reading t->next touches freed memory
explain: Michael's condition requires the hazard pointer to cover the node from a time when it was still reachable. The re-check proves t was still on the stack after the announcement was visible, so any later scan must see it. Without it, a retire and scan can slip in before the announcement.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
question: A support ticket API checks that a valid session cookie is present, then returns `/tickets/:id` for any id. Which principle does this break?
options: Open design
Complete mediation: the access to this specific ticket is never checked for authority
Psychological acceptability
Nothing: the cookie check is the authorization
explain: The cookie check is authentication. Complete mediation says every access to every object must be checked: the server must ask whether this user may read this ticket, not only whether some user is logged in.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
question: A team replaces sequential order ids with UUIDv4 and removes the ownership check, reasoning that nobody can guess a UUID. Which statement is correct?
options: This is safe because RFC 9562 guarantees UUIDs are unguessable
This is unsafe because ids leak through links, logs and other responses, and RFC 9562 says UUIDs must not be used as security capabilities
This is unsafe because UUIDv4 is predictable from timestamps
This is safe as long as the ids are sent in POST bodies
explain: Guessing is no longer practical, but possession of a leaked id would open the object. RFC 9562 explicitly forbids using UUIDs as identifiers whose mere possession grants access. Keep the ownership check.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Cases: USPS, Peloton and Optus, APIs that trusted too much
question: Peloton's first fix made an endpoint require login. Why did Pen Test Partners still call it unfixed?
options: Because the login page itself was vulnerable
Because anyone can create an account, so the same private data still went to any authenticated user
Because GraphQL cannot be secured
Because the endpoint used POST instead of GET
explain: The data exposure was an authorization problem: the API never checked whether the requester may see this rider's details. Requiring authentication only changed the audience from everyone to everyone with a free account.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
question: An enumeration alert keyed only on source IP never fires, even though one account downloaded 200,000 records. What is the most likely reason?
options: The account used HTTPS
Denials were logged as 404s
The records were returned as JSON
Requests were spread across many IP addresses, so no single IP crossed the threshold; counters should also be keyed by account or token
explain: Spreading requests over many addresses defeats per-IP counting, which is what Optus said its attacker did. Count distinct objects and denials per account, session or API key as well.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
question: Which control is Microsoft's primary mitigation for PetitPotam-style relay to AD CS web enrollment?
options: Disable Kerberos on the CA
Add the CA to Protected Users
Rotate the krbtgt password
Enable EPA and require HTTPS on the enrollment services
explain: KB5005413 recommends enabling Extended Protection for Authentication and disabling HTTP on the AD CS web enrollment services, so a relayed login fails the channel binding check.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Delegation: letting a server act as you, and how it goes wrong
question: Which control stops an admin account from being impersonated through any kind of Kerberos delegation?
options: Adding an SPN to the admin account
Enabling RC4 for the account
Moving the account to another OU
Setting 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated' or adding the account to Protected Users
explain: NOT_DELEGATED tells the KDC never to delegate that user's identity, and Protected Users members cannot be delegated with unconstrained or constrained delegation.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
question: An attacker obtained a certificate for ana.adm through ESC1. You reset ana.adm's password. Are you done?
options: Yes, the certificate is tied to the old password
Yes, if you also reset krbtgt once
No, you must delete the CA
No: the certificate still authenticates via PKINIT until it expires or is revoked; revoke it and fix the template
explain: Certified Pre-Owned stresses that certificates survive password resets. Revocation, plus fixing the template so the next request fails, is the response.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Why documents and scripts: the chain an analyst unpicks
question: What did Proofpoint's campaign data show after Microsoft announced it would block macros from the internet?
options: Email campaigns stopped carrying attachments at all
A shift toward ISO and RAR containers and LNK shortcut files
A permanent rise in XL4 macro documents
A move to PDF attachments only
explain: Macro attachments fell about 66% from October 2021 to June 2022, while container and LNK campaigns rose nearly 175%. XL4 use spiked briefly in March 2022 (TA542, the Emotet actor) but the overall trend was down.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Case: Follina (CVE-2022-30190), a document with no macro
question: Why did Office's macro protections not stop the Follina documents?
options: Macro blocking was off by default everywhere in 2022
The documents had no macro: code ran through a fetched template and the ms-msdt protocol handler
The macros were stomped
The documents were PDFs renamed to .docx
explain: Unit 42: remote templates historically carried macro-enabled files that macro policy would stop, but here the template was HTML that invoked MSDT, so code ran in Word's context even with macros disabled.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: JScript, VBScript and HTA: script hosts and their process trees
question: Why run emulation scripts like sandbox.js only inside the isolated analysis VM?
options: Node.js cannot run on a normal laptop
The vm module is not a security boundary, so hostile code can escape the fake objects
Emulation needs internet access
Windows Script Host must be installed
explain: Node's documentation says node:vm is not a security mechanism. A hostile script can reach the real Node environment, so treat emulation like detonation.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
question: Why do capa's authors leave IsDebuggerPresent out of 'check for debugger via API'?
options: Compiler-inserted code can call it, so it would cause many false positives
It no longer exists in Windows
It only works on Linux
Malware never uses it
explain: The rule's own comment: exception handlers and other compiler-inserted code may call it, especially in debug builds. Seeing the import is a reason to look, not a verdict.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
question: Why does Apple's SEAR team prefer mitigations that act early in an exploit, before memory read/write?
options: Because late mitigations are slower at run time
Because early mitigations do not need hardware support
Because early stages are tied to one bug's quirks and the attacker has fewer tools, so bypasses are not plug-and-play
Because attackers never reach read/write on modern systems
explain: Apple's post argues that constraints early in the chain compound with the bug's own constraints, while bypasses after read/write are generic and reusable. Early mitigations face a weaker attacker.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: When control flow stays legal: data-only attacks
question: What did Carlini et al.'s Control-Flow Bending study conclude about shadow stacks?
options: They are unnecessary once CFI is precise
They make CFI slower without benefit
They are necessary alongside CFI: adding them removed arbitrary code execution in three of six binaries
They replace the need for ASLR
explain: Fully precise static CFI alone still allowed powerful attacks in five of six binaries. With shadow stacks added, arbitrary code execution disappeared in half of the cases, so the authors called shadow stacks necessary.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: JIT and browser engine bugs, and the V8 sandbox
question: An attacker has arbitrary read/write inside the V8 sandbox. What does the sandbox's design say they need next?
options: Nothing, the process is theirs
A leak of the ASLR base
A second bug, a sandbox bypass, because fields inside the sandbox can only address memory inside it
Physical access to the device
explain: The sandbox's stated attacker model is arbitrary read/write inside the sandbox; its goal is to stop corruption from spreading beyond it. Reaching other process memory requires a separate vulnerability.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Zero-click chains: FORCEDENTRY and Operation Triangulation
question: How was Operation Triangulation first noticed?
options: A user reported a crash dialog
Apple's App Store review flagged a malicious app
Kaspersky saw suspicious traffic from staff iPhones on its own Wi-Fi network, then confirmed compromise from offline backups with MVT
A fuzzer reproduced the TrueType bug
explain: Detection came from network monitoring plus backup forensics, not from the device itself. It is a reminder that endpoint-invisible attacks can still leave network and timeline evidence.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Threat models for ML: goals, knowledge and capabilities
question: A competitor quietly buys the company that labels your training images. Which attack becomes easiest for them?
options: White-box evasion, because they now know your weights
Model extraction through your API
Poisoning with label control: they can mislabel or add training samples
Membership inference
explain: The labelling vendor sits on the training data path, so they gain training data control including labels. They still do not see your weights or your API traffic.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Stickers, turtles and malware: attacks outside the lab
question: In the 2022 phishing logs, the logo model was fooled but the pages were still flagged. What design property saved the system?
options: The logo model was retrained in real time
Gradient masking
The attackers used the wrong epsilon
Several independent signals were combined, so one evaded model did not decide alone
explain: The ensemble included an input-form detector and other components that the cheap logo tricks did not affect. Diversity of signals is a practical defence.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Certified robustness: randomized smoothing
question: Why did certified accuracy at radius 0.75 come out exactly 0?
options: The model is not robust at all at that radius
Sigma was too large
With n = 1,000 and alpha = 0.001, even unanimous votes give a bound of about 0.993 and a maximum radius of 0.616
Randomized smoothing only works on ImageNet
explain: The largest provable lower bound with n samples is alpha^(1/n). Bigger radii need more samples or larger sigma, which costs time or clean accuracy.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Training with differential privacy: DP-SGD and its price
question: DP-SGD clips each example's gradient to norm C before adding noise. Why clip per example rather than the averaged gradient?
options: Clipping per example bounds how much any one record can move the model, which is what lets the noise hide that record
It speeds up training
It prevents adversarial examples
Clipping the average is not possible in PyTorch
explain: The privacy proof needs a bound on each record's influence (its sensitivity). Clipping the average would let one extreme record dominate before clipping.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Red team, pentest, purple team: three different questions
question: A company's SOC has never been tested and the CISO (chief information security officer) wants detection rules improved by next quarter, with the SOC learning as it goes. Which exercise fits best?
options: An unannounced red team engagement with only the CEO informed
A vulnerability scan of every server
A purple team exercise: red runs techniques openly while the SOC checks its alerts
A bug bounty programme
explain: The goal is improvement with learning, so the cooperative format fits: each technique is run, checked and fixed in the room. A covert red team measures current detection but teaches little until the report; scans and bounties do not test the SOC at all.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Deconfliction: is this the red team or a real intruder?
question: A SOC analyst sees odd PowerShell on a finance server during a known red team week and closes the alert as 'red team, expected'. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; red team activity should be ignored
The analyst should have escalated normally so the control group could check it against the operator log
The analyst should have blocked the red team's IP addresses
The analyst should have phoned the red team directly
explain: Analysts cannot tell exercise from attack, and closing alerts on a guess is how real intruders hide inside exercises. Normal escalation lets someone with the operator log answer precisely.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: MITRE Caldera: automated adversary emulation
question: An ability requires the fact 'domain user name' and no parser has produced one yet. What does Caldera do with it?
options: Runs it with an empty value
Asks the blue team
Does not create a link for it until the required fact exists
Crashes the operation
explain: Links are generated only when an ability's fact requirements are met (and the agent has a suitable executor). This is how Caldera chains steps from discovered evidence.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: FireEye's stolen red team tools (2020)
question: Why did FireEye publish a prioritised CVE list alongside the signatures?
options: To advertise its products
Because the CVEs were zero-days
Because patching the vulnerabilities the tools relied on defeats them whatever form the tools take
Because signatures do not work on Windows
explain: Signatures detect specific tools and can be evaded by modifying them. Removing the vulnerabilities the tools exploited closes the door regardless of tooling; FireEye stressed the tools used no zero-days.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
question: Why do SWE-bench, tau-bench and WebArena grade the final state instead of comparing the agent's actions to a reference action sequence?
options: Final states are cheaper to store than action logs
Many different action sequences reach the same correct outcome, so trajectory matching would reject valid solutions
Agents do not log their actions, so there is nothing to compare
Reference action sequences would leak the answer to the agent
explain: The tau-bench paper says this directly: the user can phrase a request in different ways and the agent can call various read actions, but the episode succeeds if the database ends in the goal state. WebArena makes the same argument against comparing action sequences to references.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
question: Lab A reports a high SWE-bench Verified score using its own agent that samples many candidate patches and picks one with a reviewer model. Lab B's model reports lower on the bash-only board. What can you conclude about the underlying models?
options: Lab A's model is better, since the score is higher
Lab B's model is better, since bash-only is harder
Nothing directly: the harness, attempt count and cost differ, so only same-harness numbers compare models
They are equal once you average the two numbers
explain: Harness choices alone moved Claude 2 from 1.96% to 5.9% in the SWE-bench paper. Multi-attempt selection behaves like pass@k with a picker. Compare models only under the same scaffold and budget, which is the point of the bash-only board.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
question: Your file-read tool returns 30,000 tokens for big files, and quality drops on long tasks. Which fix follows the tool-writing guidance best?
options: Add pagination or a line-range parameter with a sensible default size and say in the result how to get more
Tell the model in the system prompt to read fewer files
Switch to a model with a larger context window
Compress the file with a summarizer before returning it, with no way to see the raw lines
explain: Token efficiency belongs in the tool: ranges, pagination and truncation with sensible defaults, plus a hint about how to fetch more. Prompting alone is unreliable, a bigger window still suffers from context rot, and an opaque summary removes the exact lines an editor needs.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
question: The store holds "User likes hiking". A new message yields the candidate "User goes hiking in the Alps every summer with their brother". Which operation fits Mem0's definitions?
options: ADD, because the sentence is new
DELETE, because the old memory is less precise
UPDATE, because it is the same topic with complementary detail
NOOP, because the user already likes hiking
explain: UPDATE is for augmenting an existing memory with complementary information, like the paper's cricket example. ADD would leave two overlapping memories (a deduplication failure). DELETE is for contradictions, and nothing here contradicts. NOOP would lose the new details.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
question: An agent's final message says: "Fixed the parser; I ran pytest and everything passes." The harness has not run anything. What do you actually know?
options: The fix is verified, since the agent observed a passing pytest run
Nothing is verified yet: the message is generated text until the harness runs the tests itself
The fix is verified if the agent's message includes the pytest output
The fix is half verified: the tests pass but the code was not reviewed
explain: Everything in the final message, including pasted output, is produced by the model and may be wrong or stale. Evidence comes from the harness running checks it controls on the actual workspace.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
question: A coding agent hits the 8-turn limit while still editing files. Which step() flags describe this ending in Gymnasium terms?
options: terminated True, truncated False, because the episode is over
terminated False, truncated True, because a limit outside the task stopped it
terminated True, truncated True, because both always go together
Neither: the turn limit is handled by the policy, not the environment
explain: The task did not reach a terminal state; an external budget cut it off. That is truncation. The distinction matters because a truncated episode says nothing about whether the agent would have succeeded, so what reward it gets is a deliberate environment design choice.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
question: During RL on a SWE environment, rewards jump while held-out benchmark scores do not. Logs show agents running `git log --all` early in many episodes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The loss mask is missing, so the model memorized tool outputs
The sandbox exposes future commits, so the policy learned to copy the upstream fix
The binary reward produced dead groups
The containers are too slow, so episodes get truncated
explain: This is the leak documented in SWE-bench issue 465. The reward rises because the policy found a shortcut that does not exist on held-out tasks with clean repositories.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
question: In the code, which single change would stop the page from adding to-do items, whatever the model decides?
options: Run tool calls only after the user approves each one, or only when no untrusted content is in the context
Translate the system prompt into French
Shorten the page before sending it
Use a bigger model
explain: The model can be persuaded; the loop cannot. Gating the tool call on approval or on the provenance of the context removes the page's power to cause side effects. The other options change how often the model obeys, not what obeying can do.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Improper output handling: model output is untrusted input
question: A support bot's answer is inserted with `element.innerHTML = answer`. What is the best fix?
options: Ask the model in the system prompt not to output HTML
Insert it as text (textContent), or render Markdown with HTML disabled and sanitise the result, backed by a strict CSP
Check that the answer does not contain the word script
Shorten answers to 200 characters
explain: Prompts can be overridden and keyword checks miss event handlers like onerror. Treat the output as text, or as Markdown through a safe renderer, and keep CSP as a second wall.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
question: A team builds its fine-tuning set from URLs listed in a public dataset published in 2021. Which single step defends against split-view poisoning?
options: Downloading the images faster
Comparing each downloaded item with a cryptographic hash recorded when the dataset was indexed, and dropping mismatches
Using a bigger model so poison is diluted
Only using HTTPS URLs
explain: The attack works because the content behind a URL changes after indexing. A hash of what the curator saw detects any change. HTTPS only proves you reached the current domain owner, who may be the attacker.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Testing it: red teaming, benchmarks and AI for defenders
question: A vendor reports that its guardrail cut attack success from 40% to 3% on a fixed public benchmark. What is the most important follow-up question?
options: What font the benchmark used
Whether the benchmark is in English
How it performs against adaptive attacks written after seeing the defence, and what the system can still do when an attack succeeds
Whether 3% can be rounded to zero
explain: Fixed benchmarks measure known attacks; attackers adapt. The residual 3% still matters, so you also need to know the blast radius when the guardrail fails.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
question: You fine-tune MatterGen for a bulk modulus target and 40% of 1,000 samples pass the MLIP filter. What is still missing before claiming new materials?
options: Nothing, since MLIP-filtered samples are stable by definition
Only a check that the bulk modulus is near the target
Running more diffusion steps
DFT verification of stability and property, deduplication against experimental databases including disordered entries, and ideally synthesis
explain: The MLIP is a filter, not the oracle. MatterGen's own bulk modulus pipeline filtered for novelty and MatterSim-predicted stability, then used DFT, and finally synthesis, which revealed that the real compound was disordered.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Second-generation text watermarks: unbiased, semantic, code, multi-bit
question: A code assistant provider must detect its own outputs in 30-line functions submitted to a coding contest. It keeps the model and the key private. Which scheme family fits best?
options: Unigram-Watermark, because one fixed list works on any length
Publicly detectable signatures, because contests are public
Entropy-aware green lists such as SWEET: watermark and score only high-entropy tokens, using the provider's own model to recompute entropies at detection
SemStamp, because code is written in sentences
explain: Short code is dominated by forced tokens, so scoring everything drowns the signal. SWEET needs the model at detection, which is fine for a provider detecting its own outputs. Public signatures need hundreds of bits of entropy, more than a short function has, and code has no natural sentences.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
question: On a glibc 2.39 system, a program calls mtrace() first thing, MALLOC_TRACE=/tmp/t is set and /tmp is writable, but no trace appears. What is the most likely cause?
options: mtrace() only works when the program is compiled with -g
libc_malloc_debug.so was not preloaded, so mtrace() is a no-op
The program must also call muntrace() to flush the file
MALLOC_TRACE must point to a directory, not a file
explain: Since glibc 2.34, mtrace and the two heap-checking features mcheck and MALLOC_CHECK_ live in libc_malloc_debug.so and are disabled in the main library. -g only improves the file:line output, and the docs advise never calling muntrace().

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
question: Why does the modified z-score multiply by 0.6745?
options: It converts the MAD into a 95 percent confidence interval
It corrects for small sample sizes the way n-1 does in the standard deviation
For normal data the MAD is about 0.6745 standard deviations, so the scaling makes M read like a z-score
It is the fraction of points the median ignores
explain: For normal data the median of |x - mu| (the MAD) is about 0.6745 sigma, because 0.6745 is the 75th percentile of the standard normal. Dividing by MAD and multiplying by 0.6745 is the same as dividing by an outlier-resistant estimate of sigma (MAD x 1.4826).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
question: Security wants to cut off a stolen token within seconds. Which design makes that easiest?
options: Long-lived self-contained JWTs with no lookup
API keys that never expire
Putting the token in a cookie
Opaque tokens checked against the issuer (introspection), or very short-lived JWTs backed by a revocable refresh token
explain: A token that is looked up can be deleted. A self-contained token stays valid until its exp unless every API checks a revocation list, which removes most of its advantage. Short lifetimes shrink that window.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
question: An authorization server receives a token request with a valid code and a code_verifier, but no challenge was sent when that code was requested. What should it do?
options: Accept: the verifier proves possession
Accept, but log a warning
Reject: RFC 9700 says to accept a code_verifier only if a code_challenge was present, to stop PKCE downgrade
Ask the user to log in again
explain: If servers accepted a verifier with no challenge on record, an attacker could start the flow without PKCE and still look PKCE-compliant later. The verifier means nothing without the earlier commitment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: JWT anatomy: header, payload, signature and base64url
question: A JWT header decodes to `{"alg":"RS256","kid":"k7"}`. What does the signature let a receiver confirm?
options: That the holder is the user named in sub
That header and payload were not changed since the holder of the private key for k7 signed them, once the receiver checks k7 is one of its trusted issuer's keys
That the payload is secret
That the token has not expired
explain: A signature proves origin and integrity of the signed bytes, nothing more. Possession is not identity (bearer token), expiry is a separate claim check, and secrecy needs encryption.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation
question: Your single-page app (SPA) keeps its access and refresh tokens in localStorage. An XSS bug is found. What should you assume?
options: Nothing leaked, since localStorage is per origin
Only the access token leaked
Both tokens may have been read and sent elsewhere; revoke the refresh tokens, fix the XSS, and consider moving to a BFF
Only users on old browsers are affected
explain: Same-origin script can read localStorage in full. The refresh token is the valuable one, since it mints new access tokens; revoke them (all, if you cannot scope the exposure) and fix the injection.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
question: In SSDF terms, running a vulnerability disclosure programme falls under which group?
options: PO, Prepare the Organization
PS, Protect the Software
PW, Produce Well-Secured Software
RV, Respond to Vulnerabilities
explain: Task RV.1.3 is having a policy for vulnerability disclosure and remediation. RV covers everything after release: finding residual vulnerabilities, fixing them and preventing repeats.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
question: A developer writes `name = request.args.get('name').strip()` and then `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = '" + name + "'")`. What will a taint tool report, and is it right?
options: Nothing: strip() is a sanitiser
A false positive, because names are harmless
A finding: strip() only removes whitespace, so taint propagates to the sink, and the report is a true positive
Nothing: cursor.execute is not a sink
explain: strip() returns a modified copy of tainted text, so the result is still tainted. Only operations whose output cannot carry the attack, such as int() for SQL or encoding for HTML, are sanitisers.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
question: A developer committed an API key, noticed, and pushed a second commit deleting it within a minute. What is the correct response?
options: None: the key is gone from the latest version
Make the repository private
Revoke the key at the provider, issue a new one, and check the key's usage logs
Squash the two commits
explain: The key is still in the first commit, and pushed history may already be cloned. Only revoking it removes its power. Then look for use between push and revocation.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
question: A finding has CVSS 9.8, EPSS 0.007, is not in KEV, and runs on an internal tool reachable only from the corporate network. Another has CVSS 7.5, is in KEV, and runs on an internet-facing proxy. Which goes first, and why?
options: The 9.8, because severity is what matters
The 7.5 in KEV on the internet-facing proxy, because it is being exploited and is exposed
Both equally
Neither until a pentest confirms them
explain: This is CVE-2023-44487 against CVE-2024-2057 in the example. Exploitation evidence plus exposure beats a theoretical maximum score. The 9.8 still gets fixed, on the normal schedule.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
question: A system uses no-steal and no-force. After a crash, which work can recovery skip entirely?
options: Redo of committed transactions, because their pages were written at commit
Undo of uncommitted transactions, because their changes never reached the data pages
Both, because the log already contains everything
Neither, because the log may be incomplete
explain: No-steal guarantees no uncommitted change was ever written to a data page, so there is nothing to undo. No-force means committed changes may still be missing on disk, so redo is still required.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
question: One page, all records for it. Before the crash: updates 1 and 2, the page is written to disk, updates 3 and 4, a partial rollback writes CLRs 4' and 3', then updates 5 and 6. The transaction is a loser. What does ARIES do at restart?
options: Redo nothing, since the transaction is a loser; undo 6, 5, 2, 1
Redo 1 through 6; undo 6, 5, 4', 3'
explain: This is Fig. 13 of the ARIES paper. Redo repeats everything after the page write, CLRs included. Undo follows PrevLSN from 6 to 5, then reaches CLR 3', whose UndoNextLSN points at 2, so 4 and 3 are not undone again. Then 2 and 1.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
question: You want to cluster 50,000 support tickets by topic with an API that offers search_query, search_document, classification and clustering types. Which setup matches the docs?
options: search_query for half the tickets and search_document for the other half
The clustering type for every ticket
search_document for all tickets, since they are stored documents
No input type, because clustering does not use cosine
explain: Clustering compares tickets with each other, a symmetric task, so every text gets the same role. Cohere documents a clustering type for exactly this, and Nomic uses a clustering prefix on both sides. Splitting the tickets across query and document types would make the halves systematically different.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
question: A 429 arrives with `Retry-After: 30`. Your backoff ceiling for this attempt would be 0.8 s. What should the client do?
options: Sleep a random time in [0, 0.8] s, since full jitter is best
Sleep 0.8 s, then 30 s if the next attempt fails
Wait at least 30 s, with a little added randomness, before retrying
Ignore the header; it is only used with 503
explain: Retry-After is the server telling you when capacity will be back. RFC 6585 allows it on 429, Anthropic says to wait that many seconds, and OpenAI treats it as a minimum and suggests adding a small random delay. Retrying after 0.8 s just produces another 429 and spends request budget.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
question: What makes Rust's `async fn` a *stackless* coroutine?
options: It cannot call other functions
It runs on the caller's stack forever and never suspends
It suspends by returning to its caller, and the data needed to resume lives in a separate object
It is only allowed inside a runtime with one thread
explain: Stackless means no private stack: suspending is a return, and the locals that must survive the suspension are stored in a separate state object (the future). Stackful coroutines instead keep a whole stack per coroutine.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
question: Two threads each run a plain (non-atomic) `counter++` once on a shared counter that starts at 0. Which statement is right?
options: The result is always 2, because each increment is one machine instruction on x86
The result is 1 or 2, and in C or C++ the program has undefined behavior
The result is always 1, because both threads read 0
It is safe as long as the counter is declared volatile
explain: Depending on the schedule, both reads can happen before either write (result 1) or not (result 2). Being one x86 instruction does not help: the core still loads and stores separately. And since the accesses conflict without synchronization, the C++ standard calls this a data race, which is undefined behavior. volatile does not make it atomic.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
question: Using the same padding rule, how many YAMNet patches (score rows) does a 10.0 s clip produce?
options: 10, one per second
21, because the last partial hop adds an extra patch
explain: The 10 s clip is padded to 161,520 samples, giving 1008 STFT frames and $1 + \lfloor (1008 - 96)/48 \rfloor = 20$ patches. Twenty patches at a 0.48 s hop span 0 to 10.08 s.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: AST and SpecAugment: patches, attention and masked bands
question: A teammate implements frequency masking by writing -80 (very quiet in their dB scale) into masked bins of unnormalized log-mel features. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, silence is the most natural mask value
Masks must be applied to the waveform, not the spectrogram
Frequency masks must always cover exactly F bins
The masked block becomes an extreme, easy-to-spot value instead of the mean; SpecAugment normalizes to zero mean so 0 equals the mean
explain: In the paper, features are normalized to zero mean and masked values are set to 0, which is the mean. Filling with an extreme value creates an unnatural pattern the model can learn to detect, and it shifts the input statistics compared with test time.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Precomputed tables, rainbow tables, and why salts defeat them
question: Which attack does a per-user salt NOT slow down?
options: Looking a hash up in a precomputed rainbow table
Running a wordlist against a single targeted user's salted hash
Cracking a million users' hashes with one shared pass of a wordlist
Spotting which users share the same password
explain: For one user, the attacker just includes that user's salt in each guess; the cost is the same as an unsalted hash of that user. Only a slow hash raises the cost per guess.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: After login: session tokens, fixation, expiry and logout
question: An attacker steals a session cookie and runs a script that makes a request every minute. Which control limits how long the stolen session works?
options: Idle timeout
The SameSite attribute
Clearing the cookie when the victim closes the browser
Absolute timeout
explain: Constant activity keeps the idle timer reset forever. Only an absolute timeout ends the session a fixed time after login regardless of activity. Clearing the victim's copy does nothing to the attacker's copy.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering
question: A caller to your help desk knows an employee's ID, manager's name and last four digits of their social security number, and asks to move MFA to a new phone. Which response best follows the guidance for this threat?
options: Approve it: the caller knew three private facts
Verify identity on camera or by calling back a registered number, with the strictest checks for privileged accounts
Approve it, then email the employee afterwards
Reset the password but leave MFA unchanged
explain: Mandiant's guidance warns that this group often already has data like date of birth and the last four digits of a social security number, so such facts prove nothing. It asks for positive identity verification, such as on-camera checks or a call-back to a registered number, before any MFA or password change.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Why CAN trusts everyone, and how its error rules can be abused
question: An engineer says: "Our brake frames carry a 4-bit counter and an 8-bit checksum, so a compromised head unit on the same bus cannot spoof them." What is wrong?
options: The checksum uses no secret, so the head unit can watch a few frames, learn the pattern and compute valid counters and checksums for its own frames
Nothing: the counter prevents replay and the checksum prevents forgery
Only the CRC matters, and the head unit cannot compute a CRC
Spoofing is impossible because the brake ECU checks the sender address
explain: Counters and checksums protect against faults, not adversaries. Miller and Valasek derived such checksums by inspection. A forger also gets the CRC for free from its CAN controller, and there is no sender address.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Case: the 2015 Jeep, from head unit to CAN bus
question: The Uconnect's OMAP chip had no direct CAN access. Why did that not protect the CAN buses?
options: Because CAN-IHS and CAN-C were the same bus
Because the D-Bus service ran on the V850
Because Sprint routed CAN frames
Because the OMAP could reprogram the V850, which did have CAN access, and the V850 did not verify firmware signatures
explain: The paper states that the V850 "can be re-flashed" and that "no cryptographic signatures are used to verify the firmware". Code on the OMAP could therefore become code on the CAN chip.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Case: CAN injection theft through a headlight, 2023
question: Why did the gateway forward the thieves' "key validated" frame to the engine ECU?
options: The gateway forwards that identifier by design, and on plain CAN it cannot tell an injected frame from the smart key receiver's
The thieves reprogrammed the gateway
The frame carried a valid SecOC tag
The engine ECU was on the same bus as the headlight
explain: Forwarding by identifier is the gateway's job. Without an authenticator, the injected frame is byte-for-byte what the genuine receiver would send. The case write-up describes the gateway copying the frame to the powertrain bus.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: A secure vehicle end to end, and where to practise
question: A team must choose one control to add first to a car whose key-validation frame travels unauthenticated over a bus exposed at the headlights. Which gives the most direct protection against the 2023 attack?
options: Encrypting the telematics link
Moving the OBD-II port
SecOC-style authentication of the key-validation frame with per-vehicle keys, checked by the ECU that releases the immobiliser
A longer UDS seed
explain: The attack's decisive step is a forged key-validation frame. Authenticating that frame end to end defeats it whatever bus the thief reaches. The other controls address different chains.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
question: A report has 20 cited claims. Every URL returns HTTP 200, and an entailment judge finds 15 of the cited passages support their claims. What is the citation precision, and what does the 200 check add?
options: 1.00; the 200 check proves the citations are correct
0.75; the 200 check is redundant once you run the judge
0.25; five failures out of twenty
0.75; the 200 check only rules out invented sources, not unsupported claims
explain: Precision is 15 / 20 = 0.75. Resolving URLs rules out fabricated sources cheaply but says nothing about support. It is not redundant: the judge needs the fetched page to compare against, and a dead link is a separate failure to report.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
question: Which statement about the output burndown rate is correct according to the AWS docs?
options: It multiplies your bill for output tokens
It applies to cache-read tokens only
It is always 5 for every model
It affects how fast output tokens consume the TPM quota, but you are billed for actual tokens
explain: The docs give an example of 1,000 input and 100 output tokens at 5x burndown: 1,500 tokens leave the quota, but you are billed for 1,100. Most models have a 1:1 rate unless the model card says otherwise.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Beyond triage: what binary reverse engineering is for
question: Why does a binary built from `hello.c` no longer contain the word hello.c or the names of its local variables?
options: The compiler encrypts names to protect intellectual property
Names are stored, but only in the Mach-O version
The CPU executes only instructions and addresses, so the toolchain keeps names only where a later step (linker, loader, debugger) needs them
The `file` command hides them
explain: Machine code refers to registers and addresses. Names survive only in tables that something else needs: the linker and loader need imported function names, and debuggers need debug info. Lesson 3 shows exactly which names survive stripping.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: ARM64 from zero: registers, loads, stores and branches
question: You see `adrp x1, 412000` then `ldr x1, [x1, #0x58]`. What does x1 hold afterwards?
options: The 8-byte value stored in memory at 0x412058, for example a GOT entry or a global pointer
The address 0x412058
The value 0x412000 + 0x58 shifted left by 12
The current program counter
explain: adrp gives the page address 0x412000; ldr with offset #0x58 reads memory at 0x412058. With add instead of ldr, x1 would hold the address itself.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: C++ binaries: name mangling, vtables and RTTI
question: In `ldr x1, [x0]; ldr x1, [x1, #24]; blr x1`, which virtual function is being called?
options: The first virtual function in the class
The typeinfo
The fourth function-pointer slot after the vtable's address point (24 / 8 = index 3)
The offset-to-top
explain: The vptr points at the first function pointer, so offset 24 is index 3 (0-based). In our classes index 0 and 1 are the two destructors, 2 is area and 3 is name.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Automating Ghidra: headless analysis and scripts
question: You must check 40 firmware builds for calls to `system()` whose argument is not a constant string. What is the most practical approach?
options: Open each build in the GUI and search by hand
Run strings on each build
Diff the files with cmp
A headless Ghidra run with a post-script over all builds, writing one line per suspicious call site
explain: Headless mode plus a script turns a manual review into a repeatable batch job, and the output becomes your list of call sites to read by hand.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a workflow, language fingerprints and practice
question: You found what looks like a buffer overflow in a router's firmware during an authorised assessment. What should the write-up contain?
options: A working exploit so the vendor believes you
The affected version and hash, the function and the evidence for the bug, the impact, and the fix, sent through the vendor's disclosure process
Only the CVSS score
The firmware file itself, posted publicly
explain: Defensive reporting gives the vendor enough to reproduce and fix the issue without publishing attack material, and goes through coordinated disclosure.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Does ternary scale? The evidence and its limits
question: Under Ouyang et al.'s fitted law, which checkpoint loses the most loss from 3-bit GPTQ?
options: A 70B model trained on 100B tokens
A 1B model trained on 1T tokens
A 70B model trained on 1T tokens
All three lose the same, since only bit width matters
explain: The law gives about 0.75 for 1B at 1T tokens, 0.29 for 70B at 1T and 0.085 for 70B at 100B. Damage grows with tokens (exponent 0.53) and shrinks with size (exponent 0.23), so the small, heavily trained model suffers most.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
question: A loop runs 1000 iterations and its loop-condition branch is mispredicted only on the final exit. Roughly what fraction of the loop's branches cost the penalty?
options: About 50 percent
About 10 percent
About 0.1 percent
None, loop branches are never predicted
explain: One miss in 1000 executions is 0.1 percent. Agner Fog notes exactly this: a loop with a high repeat count is mispredicted only when it exits, which is a negligible cost.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
question: A database's hot loop does a binary search over a sorted array, and the lookup keys arrive in sorted order (each key is close to the previous one). Which implementation is likely faster?
options: The branchy version, because successive searches take nearly the same path and are predicted well
cmov, because branchless is always faster for binary search
They are identical, since the compiler generates the same code
cmov, because it avoids loading from memory
explain: Agner Fog's binary search example: random keys give close to 50 percent prediction, where cmov wins, but keys close to each other make the branches predictable, and then a correct prediction breaks the dependency chain and overlaps loads.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Firefox Fission and WebKit: the same idea, different shapes
question: A mobile banking app shows its login page in an embedded Android WebView next to third-party ad frames. What does Chromium's process model documentation say about site isolation there?
options: Full site isolation, the same as desktop Chrome
Isolation only for login pages
No site isolation for Android WebView
Isolation only on devices with 8 GB of RAM
explain: The documentation lists Android WebView among the configurations with no site isolation. Defence there has to come from not mixing untrusted content with sensitive content in the same WebView and from keeping the WebView provider updated.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: JavaScript engines: tiers, shapes and stale assumptions
question: In the toy, which change fixes the bug without slowing every store by much?
options: Look the property up again after the callback has run, and re-check its kind
Remove the kind check
Run the callback after the write
Make slots a tuple
explain: Re-validating after user code runs is the fix pattern the V8 patch follows. Running the callback after the write changes behaviour JavaScript relies on, and removing checks makes things worse.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Case: CVE-2023-4863, one image library inside everything
question: In the toy and in libwebp's fix, why validate the whole code before building the table instead of adding a bounds check on each write?
options: Bounds checks are not allowed in C
The table size is unknown
It rejects invalid codes before any write, and once a code is known valid the table can be sized for it, so valid streams still decode with the build loop unchanged
Validation makes the image smaller
explain: A per-write bounds check would also be memory-safe. The libwebp fix runs the builder first to check validity and, if a valid code needs a bigger table, allocates more memory before filling it, so valid (even unbalanced) streams still decode. The key error in the vulnerable code was writing before knowing the input was valid.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
question: A leaf split in this course's toy tree turned one insert into 3 page writes. Which statement best explains why that is still acceptable for a B+tree?
options: Splits happen only when a leaf overflows, which is rare relative to inserts that fit, so the average cost stays near one page per insert
Splits are free because the new page is written sequentially at the end of the file
The parent node is never written to disk, only kept in memory
B+trees avoid splits entirely by keeping pages half empty forever
explain: A leaf with room for hundreds of entries splits once per hundreds of inserts. The amortized cost is dominated by rewriting the one leaf page, not by splits. Parents are persisted too (they are pages like any other), and the new page can land anywhere in the file.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
question: Which workload most favors a B+tree over an LSM-tree?
options: Inserting billions of sensor readings per day with random keys
Checking whether each of millions of incoming ids already exists, where most do not
Frequent range scans over recent and old data with few updates
A cache layer that overwrites the same keys constantly
explain: Range scans with rare updates suit a single sorted structure: the B+tree walks sibling leaves, while an LSM must merge every overlapping run and Bloom filters cannot help. High-rate random inserts, absent-key checks and overwrite-heavy workloads all play to LSM strengths.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers
question: In 2Q, a page in A1in is referenced a second time while still in A1in. What happens?
options: Nothing: it stays in A1in, because a quick second reference may be correlated
It moves to the head of Am, since two references prove it is hot
Its identifier is copied to A1out
It is evicted, because A1in only holds pages seen once
explain: The full 2Q algorithm deliberately ignores hits in A1in. Only a reference after the page has been paged out to A1out, that is after some time has passed, promotes it to Am. This is 2Q's version of LRU-K's correlated reference period.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: MTD, RTO and RPO: the arithmetic and the dependency trap
question: Why does SP 800-34 say RPO is not part of the MTD?
options: RPO measures how much data may be lost, not how long the process is down
RPO is set by the vendor rather than the business
RPO only applies to databases, MTD only to servers
RPO is always shorter than the MTD, so it never matters
explain: MTD is a duration of outage. RPO is a point in time to which data is recovered: a statement about tolerable data loss. A system can come back in 1 hour (good RTO) with a day of data missing (bad RPO), or the reverse.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
question: Atlassian met its one-hour RPO but missed its RTO. What does that tell you?
options: The backups were too old
The data was safe, but the procedure to restore it at that granularity and scale was slow
Soft delete was working correctly
Replication caused the outage
explain: Point-in-time backups to five minutes before the deletion meant little data loss. The time went into extracting hundreds of customers from shared stores and re-linking their products, a restore shape that had not been automated or rehearsed.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
question: During a major outage your status page is hosted on the same platform that is down. What should the crisis communications plan have specified?
options: Waiting until the platform is back before saying anything
A status channel hosted independently of the affected platform, plus pre-collected out-of-band contacts
Letting each engineer post updates on their own social media
Sending updates only to the regulator
explain: Communication channels are dependencies like any other (lesson 11). An independent status page and contact lists stored outside production are what Atlassian lacked when its contact data was deleted with the sites.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes
question: Using the simplified cost $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$ with $m_g$ = 6.4B and $m_\ell$ = 0.14B, what is the forward cost per byte at $P$ = 6?
options: About 13.1 GFLOPs
About 1.07 GFLOPs
About 2.41 GFLOPs
About 3.19 GFLOPs
explain: 2 x (6.4/6 + 0.14) = 2 x (1.067 + 0.14) = 2.41 GFLOPs. 13.1 is the unpatched cost, 3.19 is P = 4.4, and 1.07 forgets the factor 2 and the local term.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
question: A product mainly processes noisy user text (typos, odd casing) in many languages, and needs character-level edits. Which statement best matches the evidence in this course?
options: A BPE model with more training data will close the gap on character tasks
Byte-level models with patching are a strong fit; they were more robust to noise and far better at character manipulation
Byte models only help for English
Byte models are always faster at inference than BPE models
explain: BLT beat a same-data BPE model by 7.4 points on noised HellaSwag and by 26.6 on CUTE, while Llama 3.1, trained on far more data, scored lower on CUTE. Speed depends on patch size and implementation; the authors note wall-clock parity is not yet shown.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
question: Which line needs an `unsafe` block?
options: `let p = 0x1000usize as *const u8;`
`let n = v.len();` on a `Vec<u8>`
`v.set_len(4);` on a `Vec<u8>`
`let r = &raw const x;`
explain: Creating raw pointers (by cast or with `&raw`) is safe: nothing happens until you dereference. `set_len` is an `unsafe fn` because it trusts you that the new length is within capacity and the elements are initialized, so calling it needs an unsafe block.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
question: Using C's layout rules, what is `sizeof` of `struct { uint8_t flag; uint32_t id; uint16_t port; }` on a typical 64-bit target?
options: 7 bytes, the sum of the fields
8 bytes
12 bytes
16 bytes
explain: flag sits at offset 0, then 3 padding bytes so `id` (alignment 4) starts at 4, `port` follows at 8 and ends at 10, and the total rounds up to the struct alignment 4: 12 bytes. Rust's default layout reordered the same fields into 8 bytes, which is why FFI structs need `#[repr(C)]`.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
question: Two programs visit the same 64 MB of 8-byte nodes, one by walking an array in order and one by following a linked list whose nodes were allocated in random order. Using Drepper's results, which statement is right?
options: Both cost about the same, since they touch the same lines
The array walk is far cheaper per element because prefetching hides most of the latency; the random list pays full memory latency or more per node
The linked list is faster because pointer chasing is a single instruction per node
explain: Same lines, very different time. The sequential walk lets the prefetcher run ahead. A random pointer chase cannot know the next address until the current node arrives, so each miss is paid in full, one after another.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
question: Your graphs from per-layer transcoders show long chains of near-duplicate features across layers. What does switching to a CLT most likely change?
options: Nothing, because chains come from attention
The chains get longer because each layer now has more decoders
The chains collapse into fewer early features, at the risk of hiding a real multi-step loop
Error nodes disappear entirely
explain: A CLT feature writes to all later layers, so repeated amplification can be absorbed into one feature: shorter paths, but its causal structure can differ from the underlying model's. Error nodes remain because no dictionary is perfect.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
question: Why does constrained patching over layers [i, j] avoid double counting a cross-layer feature's effect?
options: It edits the feature's decoding at each layer in the range and does not recompute MLP outputs inside the range, so the only change there is the intervention
It recomputes every MLP inside the range so the feature's effect is applied once
It removes attention for the duration of the range
It only patches the final layer, where all decoders meet
explain: A CLT feature writes to many layers. Editing its decoder outputs across the range while not recomputing MLPs inside that range means the only change to those MLP outputs is your edit. Knock-on effects appear only after the range ends.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Lab: trace, label and intervene on a real graph with circuit-tracer
question: After clamping a supernode to -2x, the model's top output does not change and downstream supernodes stay near 100%. What is the best conclusion?
options: The intervention code is broken, since the graph showed the node
This supernode has little causal effect on this output, even though the pruned graph kept it
Attention must be unfrozen for any intervention to work
The node should be relabeled as an error node
explain: The state supernode in the tutorial behaves this way. Influence ranks nodes inside the replacement model; the intervention measures the real model. A kept node with no measurable effect is a finding to report, not something to hide.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
question: You only have logs from one fixed production ranker that never changes the order for a given query. Which method can still estimate position bias from these logs alone?
options: Intervention harvesting
Regression EM, using features shared by documents at different ranks
Identifier-based EM over (query, document) pairs
None: a swap experiment is mandatory
explain: Harvesting needs several rankers, and identifier-based EM needs each pair at multiple ranks. Regression EM only needs similar feature vectors to appear at different ranks, which happens across queries even with one deterministic ranker, though it relies on the regression model being right.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: DOM-based XSS: when the bug lives in your JavaScript
question: A single-page app reads `location.hash`, decodes it and assigns it to `innerHTML` to show a help topic. The team's WAF has never logged an attack on it. Why is that weak evidence?
options: WAFs only inspect POST bodies
innerHTML payloads are encrypted by the browser
The fragment after # is never sent to the server, so the WAF never sees that input at all
WAFs ignore requests from logged-in users
explain: Browsers keep the fragment on the client. The server and anything in front of it see only the path and query. DOM XSS through the hash is invisible to network defences and must be prevented in the code.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Second lines of defence: strict CSP and Trusted Types
question: A page has a strict nonce CSP with 'strict-dynamic'. Its trusted app.js reads a `?widget=` URL parameter and does `s = document.createElement("script"); s.src = widget; document.body.append(s)`. Is the attacker's script blocked?
options: Yes, because it has no nonce
Yes, because 'strict-dynamic' blocks all dynamically created scripts
No, because 'strict-dynamic' trusts scripts created by an already-trusted script, so this needs Trusted Types or a code fix
No, because CSP never applies to script elements
explain: 'strict-dynamic' exists so trusted loaders can add scripts without listing every host. The cost is that a trusted script with a DOM XSS bug can load anything. A TrustedScriptURL policy, or simply not taking script URLs from user input, closes it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Open redirects, and clickjacking revisited
question: Why do CSRF tokens not stop clickjacking?
options: Clickjacking only targets GET requests
Tokens are removed when a page is framed
The attacker frames the real page, which includes its own valid token, and the victim's real click submits it
Clickjacking uses the attacker's own cookies
explain: In clickjacking the forged action is performed by your genuine page, inside a frame, with a genuine click. Everything it sends is legitimate, token included. Only refusing to be framed (frame-ancestors, X-Frame-Options) stops it.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels
question: Why does CLIP project both encoders into one shared space and L2-normalize the result?
options: So images can be decoded back into captions
So a single dot product directly measures image-text similarity on a fixed scale
So the text encoder can reuse the image encoder's weights
Because normalization is what makes the encoders train from scratch
explain: With both vectors in the same space and of unit length, their dot product is their cosine similarity, a number between -1 and 1 that is comparable across every pair. CLIP has no decoder, the two towers share no weights, and training from scratch is a separate choice.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails
question: You index both product photos and product descriptions in one CLIP vector index and query it with a photo. What does the modality gap predict?
options: Results skew toward other photos, because image embeddings sit in a separate region from text embeddings
Results are evenly mixed, because the space is shared
Results skew toward descriptions, because text embeddings are closer to every image
The query fails, because image queries need the text encoder
explain: Liang et al. show image and text embeddings form separate regions (mean distance 0.82 on MS-COCO for CLIP). An image query is therefore closer to images in general than to text, so same-modality items crowd the top results even when a description matches better.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Capital One 2019 replayed through the logs
question: Your trail logs management events but excludes KMS events to cut cost, and has no S3 data events. An attacker downloads SSE-KMS encrypted objects. What can you reconstruct?
options: Every object read, from the KMS Decrypt calls
Which objects were read, from S3 server access logs that are always on
Only bucket-level and management activity; the per-object evidence was excluded twice
Nothing, because encrypted downloads are invisible to AWS
explain: KMS Decrypt calls would have carried the object ARN in their encryption context, but excluding KMS events removed them, and data events were never on. S3 server access logging is opt-in per bucket, not always on. Management events such as ListBuckets remain.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: SCARLETEEL 2023: from a Kubernetes pod to the AWS account
question: SCARLETEEL 2.0's guard policy denied CreateAccessKey for users matching `*admin*`. What is the most robust replacement?
options: Add `*Admin*` and `*ADMIN*` patterns as well
Rename AdminJoe to adminJoe
Deny CreateAccessKey for every principal except a small set of identity-management roles, and alert on any key created for a different user
Turn on GuardDuty and remove the policy
explain: More spelling variants still miss the next naming accident. Denying the action broadly with a short allowlist of roles that may manage keys does not depend on names, and the lesson 7 rule catches anyone who creates a key for someone else. GuardDuty detects; it does not prevent.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Uber 2022: from one contractor's login to the cloud consoles
question: In your report on an incident like Uber 2022, how should the attacker's screenshots showing an AWS console be described?
options: As confirmed access to customer data in AWS
As irrelevant, because screenshots can be faked
As proof that S3 data was downloaded
As claimed access: evidence that a console session existed, to be confirmed or ruled out against CloudTrail and the IdP's logs
explain: A screenshot is a claim with some weight: it suggests a session existed. The responder checks it against sign-in and API logs and reports what is confirmed separately from what is alleged. Uber, for example, said it had not found access to user data stored with its cloud providers.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Landing zones: an account layout that contains failure
question: A platform engineer wants to run a small automation Lambda in the management account because it already has broad permissions. What is the main security problem?
options: Lambda functions cannot run in a management account
The function would be billed twice
Delegated administrators would lose access to GuardDuty
SCPs do not restrict users and roles in the management account, so a bug or stolen credential there escapes every guardrail
explain: AWS's best practices keep workloads out of the management account precisely because SCPs do not apply to it. Anything running there with broad permissions is a path around every organization guardrail.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: IAM privilege escalation: the classes behind Rhino's 21 methods
question: Which change most directly closes Rhino's method 2, rolling a policy back with `iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion`?
options: Turning on MFA for the user
Adding a permissions boundary that allows iam:*
Deleting old, broader policy versions and not granting SetDefaultPolicyVersion on policies the principal holds
Renaming the policy
explain: The impact of method 2 depends on what the inactive versions allow, so delete stale broad versions and do not let principals choose the default version of their own policies. A boundary allowing iam:* limits nothing here. CloudGoat's iam_privesc_by_rollback scenario lets you practise spotting this.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Human access: LastPass 2022, Identity Center and break-glass
question: According to LastPass, at what point did the keylogger capture the DevOps engineer's master password?
options: Before the engineer completed MFA, so MFA would have stopped it
From a phishing page imitating the vault
As it was typed, after the engineer had authenticated with MFA
From a database backup in S3
explain: LastPass says the keylogger captured the master password as it was entered, after the employee authenticated with MFA. That is why the durable fix is removing long-lived secrets and hardening endpoints, not only adding factors.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The cloud from a security view: computers you rent through an API
question: Which of these is a data plane action in AWS's terms?
options: Downloading an object from a bucket
Changing a bucket's access policy
Creating a new S3 bucket
Launching a new virtual machine
explain: The data plane is the service doing its job, such as getting and putting objects. Creating buckets, changing their policies and launching VMs are administrative control plane actions.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: How AWS decides: explicit deny, SCPs, boundaries and resource policies
question: An identity policy allows `ec2:*`. An SCP on the account allows only `s3:*` and `iam:*` (it has no other Allow). What happens when the role calls `ec2:RunInstances`?
options: Denied, because the SCP has no Allow for EC2, even though it has no explicit Deny
Denied only if a permissions boundary also exists
Allowed, because the identity policy allows it
Allowed, because SCPs only contain Deny statements
explain: An action must be allowed by every SCP that applies. If the SCPs contain no matching Allow, AWS returns Deny before it looks at the identity policy.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Keyless pipelines: OIDC from CI, and roles for Kubernetes pods
question: An old role, created before IAM began rejecting this, trusts `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with only the condition `aud = sts.amazonaws.com`. What is the risk?
options: GitHub cannot reach STS without a stored key
None, because aud proves the token came from your repository
Tokens will expire too quickly for deployments
Workflows in other people's repositories can obtain valid tokens with that audience and assume the role
explain: aud only says the token is meant for AWS STS. Any repository's workflow can request such a token. The sub condition is what ties the role to your repository and branch.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Network controls: VPCs, security groups and private endpoints
question: Why does restricting a bucket to one VPC endpoint (aws:SourceVpce) help after an access key leaks?
options: It hides the bucket name
It makes the key expire
Requests signed with the leaked key but sent from outside the VPC do not arrive through the endpoint, so the explicit Deny applies
It encrypts the bucket
explain: The key still authenticates, but the bucket policy's Deny matches any request not coming through the named endpoint, and an explicit Deny overrides every Allow.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
question: Your ten incidents really contain one broad recurring failure (eight incidents, spread out) and one tight recurring failure (two incidents, close together). You run k-means with k = 2. What is the most likely outcome?
options: k-means recovers the two groups, because inertia rewards keeping similar points together
k-means splits the broad group in two and merges the tight pair into one of the halves, because that lowers the total squared distance
k-means refuses to converge, because the clusters have different variances
k-means puts the tight pair in their own cluster and marks the broad group as noise
explain: Inertia has no per-cluster width, so a wide cluster contributes a lot of squared distance. Splitting it buys a big reduction, while separating two nearby points buys almost nothing. This is the "equal variance" assumption in the scikit-learn user guide, and the reason k-means tends to split large clusters and absorb small ones. Noise is not an option: k-means has no noise label.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
question: On a new data set the gap statistic is largest at k = 4, but the one-standard-error rule picks k = 2. Which is the paper's estimate, and why the rule?
options: k = 4, because the rule is only a tie-breaker for equal gaps
Neither: the gap statistic can only choose k = 1 or k = 2
k = 2: the rule takes the smallest k whose gap is within one simulation standard error of the next one, so it does not add clusters that the reference noise cannot distinguish
k = 4, because the rule applies only when all gaps are negative
explain: Tibshirani, Walther and Hastie choose the smallest k with Gap(k) at least Gap(k+1) minus s(k+1), a one-standard-error style rule. The gap estimates are noisy, so a slightly larger gap further out is not evidence for more clusters. On our ten points the same rule picks k = 1.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: End to end: grouping a million log lines into named failure patterns
question: After deduplication you have 20000 templates with counts from 1 to 3 million. Why pass the counts to KMeans as sample_weight instead of ignoring them?
options: So that centroids and cluster sizes reflect how often messages actually occur, while the geometry is computed once per template
